Q: Return datapoints over polygons using Geopandas A:

Spatial join, then groupby and count.


import geopandas as gpd
df_poly = gpd.read_file(r"C:\GIS\GIStest\new-york-city-boroughs.geojson")
df_point = gpd.read_file(r"C:\GIS\GIStest\new_york_points.geojson")
df_poly = df_poly[["name", "geometry"]] #Keep borough name and geometry columns

#Plot
ax = df_poly.plot(column="name", categorical=True, figsize=(10,10), cmap="Set1")
df_point.plot(ax=ax, color="cyan", zorder=2, edgecolor="black", markersize=80)
_ = df_poly.apply(lambda x: ax.annotate(xy=(x.geometry.representative_point().x,
                                            x.geometry.representative_point().y),
                                        text=x["name"], 
                                        color="black", 
                                        size=18), axis=1)

#Spatial join points to polygon, groupby borough name, count points and save as dict
point_count = df_poly.sjoin(df_point, how="left",  predicate="intersects").groupby(
    "name")["index_right"].count().to_dict()

#print(point_count)
#{'Bronx': 0, 'Brooklyn': 1, 'Manhattan': 0, 'Queens': 8, 'Staten Island': 3}

df_poly["n_trips"] = df_poly["name"].map(point_count)
# print(df_poly[["name", "n_trips"]])
#             name  n_trips
# 0  Staten Island        3
# 1         Queens        8
# 2       Brooklyn        1
# 3      Manhattan        0
# 4          Bronx        0

Q: UDP sendto() succeeds but outgoing UDP packet is not transmitted while receiving 500 Mbps UDP stream on Windows A:

sendto() succeeding only means Winsock (Windows Sockets) accepted the datagram into its buffer for transmission, it does not guarantee that the packet has reached the NIC driver or gone out onto the physical wire.

Since this issue persists across both Python and PowerShell, the bottleneck is almost certainly below the application layer in the NIC/NDIS driver stack. At a ~500 Mbps incoming stream rate, receive-side processing, DPC/interrupt moderation load, or NIC queue congestion can starve or drop outgoing packets after Winsock accepts them.

Furthermore, do not rely solely on Wireshark on the sending host to prove the packet wasn't transmitted. Under heavy traffic (~500 Mbps), Npcap (Wireshark's packet capture driver) can drop capture events in the kernel buffer even if the NIC actually sends the frame out.

A few things worth trying to isolate and fix the issue:

  • Capture externally: Sniff traffic on the receiving host (FPGA/network switch port) rather than relying on Wireshark on the sending machine.

  • Check NIC Driver Settings:

    • Enable RSS so incoming UDP processing is distributed across multiple CPU cores rather than pinning a single core.

    • Adjust Interrupt Moderation or temporarily disable UDP Checksum Offload / Large Send Offload (LSO) in the NIC advanced properties to see if the driver is bottlenecking.

  • Dedicated Control Socket/Port: you could also try using a dedicated, persistent UDP socket bound to a separate port exclusively for outgoing STOP commands rather than recreating threads or sharing the high-throughput receive socket.

Q: How do you learn coding today? A:

The reason everything feels like a haze is because copy-pasting AI code cuts out the most important part of learning: debugging the mess you made.

When you write code yourself and it breaks, you spend an hour reading terminal logs, searching docs, and understanding why it failed. That pain is what builds intuition. When Claude generates a working script, you skip the struggle, so nothing sticks.

Here is how to bridge the gap between "vibe coding" and actual engineering:

1. Treat Claude as a junior dev, not an oracle

Don't ask it to "build a pipeline." Ask it to explain concepts or draft small snippets. Rule of thumb: Never paste code you couldn't rewrite from scratch if someone took away your internet. If Claude gives you a 50-line Dockerfile and you don't know what 3 of those flags do, stop and look up those 3 flags before moving on.

2. Learn by breaking stuff

Production-grade code isn't about writing logic that works on a sunny day; it's about handling what happens when things fail. Take a working project generated by Claude and intentionally break it:

  • Kill the database connection mid-request.

  • Pass invalid/corrupted JSON to your API.

  • Revoke environment variables in your Docker container.

Now, turn off Claude and try to fix it just by reading the terminal logs and stack traces. Learning how to read raw error logs is 80% of what separates a beginner from someone who can maintain production software.

3. Focus on the production wrapper, not the ML logic

Since you already have a Data Science background, stop focusing on the model code. Focus entirely on what wraps around it:

  • Logging: Swap print() for structured logs.

  • Validation: Use Pydantic schemas to strictly validate every input.

  • Environment: Containerize it with Docker so it runs the exact same way on your laptop as it does on a cloud VM.

  • Handling failures: What happens if the API times out? Add retries and proper error responses.

Bottom line

You don't need to stop using Claude, but use it as interactive documentation rather than an automated code factory. If you can't explain every architectural decision and failure point in your repo to an interviewer on a whiteboard, you don't actually own the code yet.

Q: How to mock a method that returns an asynchronous iterator in a test using pytest-mock? A:

fetch_members() returns an async iterator; it is not something you await. The issue is that patch() created a normal mock whose call result is being treated as a coroutine.

Mock the method so it directly returns an async iterable:

async def members():
    yield mock_member

mock_guild = mocker.MagicMock()
mock_guild.fetch_members.return_value = members()
await scraper.activate(mock_guild)

Or configure __aiter__ directly:

mock_guild = mocker.MagicMock()
mock_guild.fetch_members.return_value.__aiter__.return_value = [mock_member]

Also, there is no need to patch discord.Guild.fetch_members globally if you already pass a mocked guild into activate(). Mocking the instance is simpler and avoids confusing coroutine behaviour. Guild.fetch_members() is documented as returning an asynchronous iterator.

Q: How to get continuous smooth/average of contour in OpenCV? A:

Here is one way in Python OpenCV.

  • Read the input

  • Convert to grayscale

  • Threshold and invert

  • Apply morphology open to separate a moderate size blob in the upper left from the main blob

  • Get the largest contour

  • Draw the contour as white filled on a black background

  • Pad the image on all sides by a large amount

  • Apply morphology close with a large kernel to smooth the boundary

  • Crop the previous image back to its original size

  • Find the largest contour

  • Draw the contour on a copy of the input

  • Save images

Input image:

import cv2
import numpy as np

# read input image
img = cv2.imread('dark_blob.png')

# convert to grayscale
gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

# threshold to binary and invert
thresh = cv2.threshold(gray, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY_INV+cv2.THRESH_OTSU)[1]

# apply morphology open
kernel = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_ELLIPSE, (5,5))
morph_open = cv2.morphologyEx(thresh, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, kernel)

# find largest contours
contour_img = img.copy()
contours = cv2.findContours(morph_open, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
contours = contours[0] if len(contours) == 2 else contours[1]
big_contour = max(contours, key=cv2.contourArea)

# draw contour on copy of input
cntr_img = img.copy()
cv2.drawContours(cntr_img, [big_contour], 0, (0,0,255), 2)

# draw white filled contour on black background
cntr_img2 = np.zeros_like(thresh)
cv2.drawContours(cntr_img2, [big_contour], 0, 255, -1)

# pad the image by 100 all around
pad = 200
pad_img = cv2.copyMakeBorder(cntr_img2, pad,pad,pad,pad, borderType=cv2.BORDER_CONSTANT, value=(0))

# apply morphology close
kernel = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_ELLIPSE, (200,200))
morph_close = cv2.morphologyEx(pad_img, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, kernel)

# crop out the 100 all around
hh, ww = morph_close.shape[:2]
crop_img = morph_close[pad:hh-pad, pad:ww-pad]

# # find largest contours
contour_img = img.copy()
contours = cv2.findContours(crop_img, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
contours = contours[0] if len(contours) == 2 else contours[1]
big_contour = max(contours, key=cv2.contourArea)

# draw contour on copy of input
result = img.copy()
cv2.drawContours(result, [big_contour], 0, (0,0,255), 2)

# save result
cv2.imwrite("dark_blob_thresh.jpg", thresh)
cv2.imwrite("dark_blob_morph_open.jpg", morph_open)
cv2.imwrite("dark_blob_contour1.jpg", cntr_img)
cv2.imwrite("dark_blob_contour2.jpg", cntr_img2)
cv2.imwrite("dark_blob_crop_image.jpg", crop_img)
cv2.imwrite("dark_blob_result.jpg", result)

# show images
cv2.imshow("thresh", thresh)
cv2.imshow("morph open", morph_open)
cv2.imshow("contour1", cntr_img)
cv2.imshow("contour2", cntr_img2)
cv2.imshow("pad image", pad_img)
cv2.imshow("crop image", crop_img)
cv2.imshow("result", result)
cv2.waitKey(0)

Q: Why can adding logging make a Python race condition disappear? A:

Regarding your question "what is a reliable way to reproduce and debug these timing-dependent bugs without accidentally changing the behavior I'm trying to observe?" You can use:

time.sleep(0)

This can make the race condition easier to reproduce by giving other thread an opportunity to run between the read and the write.

Q: Using a regex as a template with Python A:

The subject is old, but I just had exactly the same need, and found no library doing it.

So I added the feature in the library HolAdo that I maintain. In file src/holado_python/common/tools/re_ext.py is method pattern_to_format_string that converts a regex pattern to a f-string:

if sys.version_info < (3, 11, 0):
    import sre_parse as re_parser
else:
    import re._parser as re_parser


def pattern_to_format_string(pattern):
    if isinstance(pattern, re.Pattern):
        pattern = pattern.pattern
    if not isinstance(pattern, str):
        raise Exception(f"Pattern argument [{pattern}] is not a string or a re.Pattern")

    parsed_pattern = re_parser.parse(pattern)
    group_name_by_index = {v:k for k,v in parsed_pattern.state.groupdict.items()}

    res = ""
    for node_index, node in enumerate(parsed_pattern.data):
        match node[0]:
            case re_parser.AT:
                pass
            case re_parser.LITERAL:
                c = chr(node[1])
                res += c
                # Escape formatter characters
                if c in ['{', '}']:
                    res += c
            case re_parser.SUBPATTERN:
                pattern_index = node[1][0]
                if pattern_index in group_name_by_index:
                    res += "{" + group_name_by_index[pattern_index] + "}"
                else:
                    raise Exception(f"Pattern with unnamed group is not managed in root nodes (node index: {node_index} ; parsed pattern: {parsed_pattern})")
            case _:
                raise Exception(f"Pattern root nodes can only be literals or named groups ; got a node of type [{node[0]}] (node index: {node_index} ; parsed pattern: {parsed_pattern})")

    return res

For your example it becomes:

import re
from holado_python.common.tools.re_ext import pattern_to_format_string

pattern = re.compile("/something/(?P<id>.*)")
pattern_format = pattern_to_format_string(pattern)
pattern_format.format(id=1)
